newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian Premier Hun Sen says 12 hostages dead.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian Premier Hun Sen says 12 hostages dead.

text.p: Cambodian Co-Premier Hun Sen said on Thursday that intelligence reports indicated that 12 out of 15 government staff held by Khmer Rouge guerrillas for the past month were dead.
Hun Sen, speaking at a farmers' day ceremony in the eastern Cambodian province of Kompong Cham, did not say how the 12 had died.
He added that the fate of British mine clearance expert Christopher Howes, who was abducted by rebels nearly one year ago, was uncertain.

The 15 hostages, most of them from co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, flew by helicopter into territory held by hardline Khmer Rouge guerillas on February 14 to conduct negotiations on defections by the rebels.
"There are only three people alive, including one pilot," said Hun Sen of the 15 government staff, who included Deputy Governor Hem Bunheng of Siem Reap province
Hun Sen said he had received the information through intelligence reports, but hoped the information was not true.
The 15 staff were being held in or near the northern Cambodian base of Anlong Veng by hardliners under feared Khmer Rouge military chief Ta Mok. Howes, if alive, is also thought to be in Anlong Veng.
Ranariddh and other officials have ordered Ta Mok to release the hostages soon or face attack, while the government has built up its forces around Anlong Veng since the beginning of the month.
"Now we have some 10,000 soldiers around Anlong Veng," a senior FUNCINPEC military official told reporters on Thursday.
He said the soldiers' task would be easier than last year, before the Khmer Rouge had been crippled by thousands of defections.
The Khmer Rouge rebels are now believed to number fewer than 2,000 fighters, most of them in and around Anlong Veng.
The Maoist-inspired guerrillas signed a U.N.-sponsored peace pact in 1991, but reneged on the deal and have been fighting the coalition government formed after 1993 elections.

Hun Sen questioned the wisdom of the February 14 FUNCINPEC mission and negotiations with Ta Mok, dubbed "The Butcher" for abuses during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule which left more than one million people dead.
"Why negotiate with Ta Mok? Who is responsible for the tragedy? It is not the work of the government," he told villagers, government and business officials at the ceremony.
Air force pilots at an air show attended by Ranariddh on Thursday said they were studying maps of the Anlong Veng area and were ready to attack the rebels.
Ranariddh insisted on Thursday the negotiations with the Khmer Rouge rebels were going well, but did not comment on the welfare of the hostages.
